title: There's No Marquis in 'A Friend of the Marquis'
standfirst: The nobleman in this 1875 panel's title never appears in it, and even the two people who do are a dispute Boldini's own cataloguers can't settle. He built pictures like this one to a formula, for a market that wanted the eighteenth century without having lived through it — a year before he abandoned the recipe for good.

sections.heading: The Marquis Never Sits for His Own Portrait
sections.body:
The title promises a marquis. What the panel actually holds is a woman crossing a mirrored gallery in a green floral gown and a man sprawled on a striped settee, cane in hand, neither one labelled, neither one obviously titled. The marquis of the title never appears in the frame at all — he exists only as the absent third party who gives the other two their relationship to each other, and to him.

Even that relationship is contested before you get past the title. [WikiArt](https://www.wikiart.org/en/giovanni-boldini/a-friend-of-the-marquis-1875) records the original Italian as *L'amica del marchese* — the marquis's female friend, which puts the woman at the centre of the sentence. A stock-photography agency's [caption for the same picture](https://www.alamy.it/giovanni-boldini-amico-del-marchese-dipinto-ad-olio-su-pannello-1875-image463523782.html), dated to the same year on the same oil-on-panel support, calls it *amico del Marchese* instead — masculine, which hands the title to the seated man and leaves the woman as someone else's business entirely. Two archives, one picture, and neither will settle which figure in it is actually the friend.

sections.heading: Boldini Was Manufacturing Aristocrats to Order
sections.body:
By 1875, Boldini had been in Paris for four years, having taken a studio near the Place Pigalle in October 1871 after training in Florence ([Stephen Ongpin Fine Art](https://www.stephenongpin.com/object/834541/0/giovanni-boldini-ferrara-1842-paris); [Culturius](https://magazine.culturius.com/en/boldini-the-painter-of-elegance/)). Almost as soon as he arrived he attached himself to Adolphe Goupil, whose Paris house had spent decades building one of the largest export operations in European art — a print-and-picture business with a London branch and, from the late 1840s, a shopfront on Broadway, selling French taste to buyers who would never see the Salon in person ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolphe_Goupil); [Stephen Ongpin Fine Art](https://www.stephenongpin.com/artist/236471/giovanni-boldini)).

What Goupil wanted from Boldini through the 1870s was not modern Paris. It was an invented eighteenth century: small, tightly finished panels of powdered wigs and rococo boiserie, peopled by figures who carry titles instead of names — *A Friend of the Marquis*, *Ladies of the First Empire*, *A Lute Player and a Listener*, *Gossip* ([Wikipedia's list of his works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_works_by_Giovanni_Boldini)). None of them are identified sitters; they are stock characters, built to a formula an export house could sell without a story attached. One eventual buyer of Boldini's smaller early work, decades on, was the American collector Robert Sterling Clark, whose taste a curator at his own institute has summed up as wanting art that was ["trendy, but not too far out"](https://www.berkshireeagle.com/news/local/rediscovering-giovanni-boldini/article_677a3b04-44ba-5c09-b5f0-5086931d807f.html) — a description this marquis and his unnamed friend fit rather well.

sections.heading: A Provincial Realist Learned to Fake the Ancien Régime
sections.body:
Boldini was born in Ferrara on 31 December 1842, the eighth of thirteen children of a painter who worked mostly as a copyist ([Culturius](https://magazine.culturius.com/en/boldini-the-painter-of-elegance/)). Wikipedia dates his move to Florence to study painting to 1862; two dealers who have separately handled his work give 1864 instead ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Boldini); [Stephen Ongpin Fine Art](https://www.stephenongpin.com/artist/236471/giovanni-boldini); [The Eclectic Light Company](https://eclecticlight.co/2015/05/06/beyond-the-french-impressionists-2-the-macchiaioli-giovanni-boldini/)) — a two-year gap in an artist this documented that nobody seems to have bothered closing.

What isn't disputed is the circle he joined there: the Macchiaioli, meeting at the Caffè Michelangiolo, painting outdoors and against the academy in blocks of tone rather than finished line. Boldini's closest ties were to Telemaco Signorini and to Cristiano Banti, and among his patrons in these years was the critic Diego Martelli, the group's most committed champion ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Boldini)). It is a strange training for the man who would spend the following decade painting rococo interiors nobody in that Florentine circle had any interest in reviving — realism, learned outdoors, retooled indoors to sell an aristocracy that was already a century dead by the time he touched it.

sections.heading: 1876 Is the Year He Burned This Recipe
sections.body:
This panel is dated 1875. The following year, by the account of specialists who track Boldini's brushwork rather than his subject matter, he abandoned the style it is painted in almost entirely. Through the early 1870s his surfaces had stayed close to the rigorously realist, highly finished manner he had brought from Florence; by 1876 he had swapped it for brighter colours at higher chroma, laid down in rapid bravura brushstrokes — the loose, slashing hand that would earn him the nickname "Master of Swish" for the rest of his career ([The Eclectic Light Company](https://eclecticlight.co/2015/05/06/beyond-the-french-impressionists-2-the-macchiaioli-giovanni-boldini/)).

That makes this picture one of the last full products of the old method — tight enough in its rendering of gilt and brocade that a buyer could mistake it for an actual eighteenth-century curiosity, rather than the fast, visible-brushstroke performance Boldini would be selling within two years. The costume in the painting is fake. In 1875, so was the brushwork's spontaneity; both were still under total control.

sections.heading: The Portraitist He Became Buried the Forger He'd Been
sections.body:
By the 1890s, Boldini was the most sought-after portrait painter in Paris, a friend of Edgar Degas and later of John Singer Sargent, painting real aristocrats and heiresses under his own name rather than inventing anonymous ones for export ([Stephen Ongpin Fine Art](https://www.stephenongpin.com/artist/236471/giovanni-boldini); [Modernist Journals Project](https://modjourn.org/biography/boldini-giovanni-1842-1931/)). That later fame is so complete that the 1870s export trade — the small panels, the invented marquises, the Goupil pipeline to American money — barely survives as a chapter in his story, let alone in how this specific period gets catalogued now.

This picture is filed, in the record behind this page, under Impressionism. A specialist assessment of exactly this stretch of Boldini's career disagrees: he "remained on the periphery" of that movement, never showed in its group exhibitions, and borrowed its habits without joining its argument ([The Eclectic Light Company](https://eclecticlight.co/2015/05/06/beyond-the-french-impressionists-2-the-macchiaioli-giovanni-boldini/)). Add a title whose gender changes depending which archive you trust, and a training date that shifts by two years between sources, and the honest description of this painting's paperwork is not Impressionist, not Rococo-revival, not really genre painting either. It is simply unsettled — which, for a picture built to be sold rather than remembered, is about right.
